intro: Kasama is a pottery town in the hills of central Ibaraki, north-east of Tokyo. At Inada, on its western side, stands Sainen-ji, the temple built where the monk Shinran kept a thatched hut in the early thirteenth century. In its grounds grows a leaf-seed ginkgo that Ibaraki Prefecture protects as a natural monument, 7.5 metres round and 35 metres tall. A reader sent it to us for its autumn colour.
meta_description: The leaf-seed ginkgo of Sainen-ji at Inada, Kasama: a prefectural natural monument 7.5 metres round, said to date from Shinran's hut of 1218.

trees.name: The Leaf-Seed Ginkgo of Inada Gobo

location.address: Sainen-ji (Inada Gobo), 469 Inada, Kasama, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan

trees.story:
By the temple's own account, this ginkgo was planted around 1218, when the monk Shinran built a thatched hut at Inada. He lived there for years, and the temple says he worked on his main book, the Kyogyoshinsho, in that hut. The temple that grew on the spot is Sainen-ji, also called Inada Gobo, and the tree still stands in its grounds.

It is an ohatsuki ginkgo, a rare form that sets some of its seeds on the edges of its leaves instead of on stalks of their own. Ibaraki Prefecture made it a natural monument in November 2000. Its record gives a trunk 7.5 metres round, a height of 35 metres and a crown 23 metres across, and says no other leaf-seed ginkgo in the prefecture has a wider trunk, the national monument at Mito's Hachimangu included. It also calls the tree vigorous.

The prefecture puts its age at more than 300 years, the cautious figure, and the reader who sent it to us says about 300 as well. The planting date of 1218 is the temple's own story, and nobody has measured it.

That reader also told us when to come. In autumn, they say, its colours are spectacular. The grounds are free to walk into by day, about fifteen minutes on foot from Inada Station.

question_meta: The oldest tree we know of in Kasama is the leaf-seed ginkgo of Sainen-ji at Inada, more than 300 years old by the prefecture's record.
question_answer: The leaf-seed ginkgo in the grounds of Sainen-ji (Inada Gobo) at Inada, Kasama. Ibaraki Prefecture puts it at more than 300 years old, and temple tradition says it was planted around 1218.
question_context: Sainen-ji, also called Inada Gobo, stands where the monk Shinran kept a thatched hut in the early thirteenth century, the base from which he taught across the Kanto and, the temple says, worked on the Kyogyoshinsho. Temple tradition holds that the ginkgo in its grounds was planted around 1218, in Shinran's time there. Ibaraki Prefecture, which made it a natural monument in November 2000, is more cautious and gives its age as more than 300 years. Its record measures the trunk at 7.5 metres round, the height at 35 metres and the crown at 23 metres across, and says no other leaf-seed ginkgo in the prefecture has a wider trunk. A leaf-seed ginkgo, ohatsuki icho in Japanese, is a rare form that sets some of its seeds on the edges of its leaves. The reader who told us about it says it is about 300 years old and that its autumn colours are spectacular. The temple grounds are free to visit from 9:00 to 16:30, about fifteen minutes on foot from JR Inada Station.
